role: Independent expert, blind solve (production-plan.md section 5, steps 2 and 3). Coach only; never published.
method: Each item read from the served question alone: tools/mock/data/full-mocks.js loaded in a node vm exactly as scripts/explainers/build.mjs does, printing stem, stem figure (qs), structure-choice flag (os) and choices in served order, with the key, why and traps fields withheld.
The full-mock player (tools/mock/full.js) serves choices in bank order with no shuffle; the copy served at http://127.0.0.1:4107/ hashes the same as the file on disk.
Blind picks were saved before any key was loaded; keys were compared after; the bank why and trap notes were read only after that, for the writer notes.

Every number recomputed (the X-linked cross enumerated, the map-distance conversion, the ATP tally and each distractor route). RDKit not applicable: no item in this batch has a structure in its stem or choices. No RC items, so no proof lines.

items.expertAnswer: All sons affected, all daughters carriers
items.servedKey: All sons affected, all daughters carriers
items.concept: X-linked recessive inheritance: a son gets his only X from his mother, so an affected mother has all affected sons and carrier daughters (criss-cross).
reasoning: Write the parents: an affected mother is Xc Xc (both X chromosomes carry it); the father is XC Y.
Every child gets an Xc from the mother. Sons get the Y from the father, so every son is Xc Y and affected.
Daughters get the father's XC, so every daughter is XC Xc: normal vision, carrier.

choices.text: All daughters affected and all sons unaffected
choices.misconception: Swaps which sex gets which X. The father gives daughters his normal X and gives sons only a Y.
The 1 in 4 of an autosomal carrier by carrier cross. Here the mother's allele goes to every child, so nothing is left to chance.
True of the daughters' vision, not the sons. Thinks sons take an X from the father.
Applies the rule that one normal dominant allele masks a recessive trait. Sons have one X and nothing to mask it.

choices.text: All sons affected, all daughters carriers
choices.why: Sons: Xc from mother plus Y. Daughters: Xc from mother plus XC from father.

writerNotes: Choice texts are shorthand and not parallel (25% affected each; No effect). A stem-style flag candidate for Thomas; rewording suggested, never applied.

items.concept: The genetic code is redundant; point mutations are named by what happens to the protein (silent, missense, nonsense), frameshifts by an insertion or deletion.
reasoning: Read what changed: one base pair swapped, protein sequence identical.
Know the code is redundant: several codons spell the same amino acid, often differing only at the third base.
Name it by the protein outcome: same protein means silent.

choices.misconception: The substitution class next door, where the new codon spells a different amino acid, so the sequence would change.

choices.why: The new codon is a synonym for the same amino acid.

choices.misconception: Comes from inserting or deleting bases in a number not divisible by three. A single substitution keeps the reading frame.
The case where the new codon is a stop, which cuts the protein short.
Names the base chemistry (purine for pyrimidine), not the protein outcome the stem asks about.

writerNotes: A silent change can itself be a transition or a transversion, so the Transversion note should say it answers a different question (the chemistry), not that it cannot be true.

items.concept: Map units: 1 centimorgan is defined as 1 percent recombinant offspring, and observed recombination tops out at 50 percent.
reasoning: Know the definition: 1 map unit (centimorgan) equals 1 percent recombinant offspring.
So 25 centimorgans reads straight across as 25 percent recombinants, under the 50 percent ceiling.
The three-point setup does not change the conversion.

choices.misconception: Shrinks the distance as if centimorgans needed a conversion first. No clean misconception sits behind this value.
Halves the distance, as if the half-the-chromatids correction were still owed. The centimorgan already is percent recombinants.

choices.why: Centimorgans are defined as percent recombinants.

choices.misconception: The value for genes that assort independently (unlinked, or very far apart).
The parental (nonrecombinant) share, 100 minus 25. Also above the 50 percent ceiling.

writerNotes: The bank why points to "the word approximate", which this stem does not contain (bank-copy note; the bank is not edited).

Nuance to keep out of the explainer: for outer markers in a real three-point cross, undetected double crossovers make the observed frequency read a little under the map distance. At DAT level 25 cM is 25 percent; do not claim more precision.
The 5% choice has no real misconception behind it (decisions doc: every distractor from a real misconception). Flag for a later rewrite; key unchanged.

items.concept: CO2 + H2O <-> H2CO3 <-> H+ + HCO3-: ventilation sets CO2, so breathing changes pH, and a lung-caused shift is labeled respiratory.
reasoning: Follow the CO2: rapid deep breathing at rest blows off CO2.
Less CO2 pulls the carbonic acid equilibrium to the left, using up H+, so pH rises: alkalosis.
The lungs caused it, so the label is respiratory.

choices.misconception: Cause and effect swapped: metabolic acidosis drives fast breathing as compensation; it is not caused by it.
The outcome of hypoventilation, where CO2 is retained and pH falls.

choices.text: Metabolic alkalosis from a loss of hydrogen ions
choices.misconception: Alkalosis holds, but the cause is CO2 lost through the lungs, not H+ lost from the gut (as in vomiting).
Sees the breathing change but stops before following CO2 through carbonic acid to H+. Ventilation moves pH within minutes.

choices.why: Blowing off CO2 lowers H+; the lungs caused it.

items.confidenceNote: High on the answer: it is the only defensible choice. The key text mixes two gland types (see writer notes).
items.concept: Sweat glands are not evenly spread: eccrine glands are densest on the palms and soles (forehead next), and the axillae hold the apocrine glands.
reasoning: Know the map: eccrine sweat glands are densest on the palms and soles, several hundred per square centimeter.
The axillae are where the apocrine sweat glands concentrate, so the choice naming palms, soles and axillae is the concentrated set.
Cross off the even-spread claim and the low-density sites (back, eyelids, lips).

choices.misconception: A large surface that can shed a lot of sweat in total, but its gland density is low. Total output is not density.

choices.why: Palms and soles lead for eccrine glands; the axillae hold the apocrine glands.

choices.text: Spread at the same density over the entire body surface
choices.misconception: Treats every region as equal when density differs several-fold from palm to trunk.
The lid margin's glands are mostly oil-making; eyelid skin carries few sweat glands.
The lip margin has essentially no sweat glands, so lips sit at the bottom of the ranking, not the top.

writerNotes: Do not write that the axillae are among the densest sites for eccrine glands. Eccrine density leads on the palms, soles and forehead; the axillae are listed because of their apocrine glands. The bank why says densest on palms, soles and axillae without that split.
Not a key dispute: no other choice is defensible. For Thomas, optional: the key text could later name the gland types; any change is his, in the bank.

items.concept: Gastric gland cells by product: parietal cells make HCl (via the H+/K+ ATPase) and intrinsic factor; chief cells pepsinogen; mucous cells mucus; G cells gastrin.
reasoning: Sort the stomach lining by product: parietal for acid, chief for pepsinogen, mucous neck and surface cells for mucus, G cells for gastrin.
The acid maker is the parietal cell, with its H+/K+ ATPase proton pump.

choices.misconception: Chief cells release pepsinogen, the enzyme precursor the acid then activates.
Mucus-secreting cells of the intestine and airways.

choices.why: The proton pump of the parietal cell secretes H+ with Cl- following.

choices.misconception: They make the mucus that shields the lining from the acid.
G cells release gastrin, the signal that tells parietal cells to make acid. Picking them stops one step before the acid source.

items.concept: Sodium handling along the nephron: the proximal tubule reclaims the bulk (about two thirds, water following), the thick ascending limb about a quarter, and the distal end fine-tunes the last few percent.
reasoning: Picture the filtered sodium as a budget the nephron spends down.
The proximal convoluted tubule does the bulk: about two thirds, with water following.
Then the thick ascending limb takes about a quarter, and the distal tubule and collecting duct fine-tune the last few percent.

choices.misconception: The thick ascending limb's share, the second-largest site.
Splits the work roughly evenly across the tubule instead of giving the proximal tubule the bulk.
The distal tubule's fine-tuning share.

choices.why: The proximal tubule reclaims about two thirds of filtered sodium.

choices.misconception: Close to the whole-nephron total, not the proximal tubule alone.

writerNotes: A recall number. Teach the shape first (bulk early, fine-tuning late), then the number.
The ~45% choice has a weak misconception behind it; flag for a later rewrite, key unchanged.

items.concept: Glomerular filtration is pressure-driven bulk flow: glomerular capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes out, opposed by plasma colloid osmotic pressure and capsule pressure.
reasoning: Name the forces at the glomerulus: capillary blood (hydrostatic) pressure pushes fluid out; plasma protein (colloid osmotic) pressure and capsule pressure push back.
A wide afferent and a narrower efferent arteriole hold glomerular hydrostatic pressure high, so it wins.
That is bulk flow with no ATP spent: hydrostatic pressure.

choices.text: Colloid osmotic pressure of the plasma proteins
choices.misconception: It opposes filtration, pulling fluid back into the capillary.
Active transport works later, in tubular reabsorption, not in filtration.
Aquaporins are water channels in the collecting duct under ADH control. There is no aquaporin gradient driving filtration.

choices.why: Glomerular capillary blood pressure drives bulk flow into the capsule.

choices.misconception: Diffusion moves solutes down their own gradients, as in gas exchange; filtration pushes water and small solutes together.

writerNotes: "Aquaporin gradient" is not a real term, so this choice reads as filler rather than a misconception; flag for a later rewrite, key unchanged.

items.concept: Alcoholic fermentation in yeast: pyruvate loses CO2 to become acetaldehyde, which takes NADH's electrons to become ethanol, regenerating NAD+.
reasoning: Name the pathway: yeast without oxygen run alcoholic fermentation.
Pyruvate loses CO2, the gas that lifts the dough, and becomes acetaldehyde.
Acetaldehyde takes NADH's electrons and becomes ethanol, the alcohol that bakes off; NAD+ is regenerated.

choices.misconception: Lactate fermentation (muscle, some bacteria) releases no gas, so nothing would lift the dough.

choices.why: CO2 lifts the dough; ethanol bakes off.

choices.misconception: The aerobic link reaction also releases CO2 from pyruvate, but makes acetyl-CoA, not ethanol.
Pyruvate is where glycolysis ends and fermentation starts; yeast release no hydrogen gas.
Ethanol holds, but fermentation neither uses nor makes oxygen.

items.concept: The glycolysis investment phase: hexokinase and phosphofructokinase-1 each move a phosphate from ATP onto the sugar; the payoff kinases make ATP.
reasoning: Find the first-half steps where a kinase moves a phosphate from ATP onto the sugar: there are two.
Glucose to glucose-6-phosphate (hexokinase), and fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate (phosphofructokinase-1).
The payoff kinases, phosphoglycerate kinase and pyruvate kinase, make ATP instead.

choices.misconception: The payoff pair: one makes NADH and the other makes ATP, so they earn rather than spend.
Hexokinase spends ATP, but pyruvate kinase is a payoff enzyme that makes ATP.
First-half steps right after the spending: they split and reshuffle the sugar with no ATP.
A rearrangement and a dehydration; neither touches ATP.

choices.why: The two first-half kinases each spend one ATP.

writerNotes: The bank why gives "a phosphate goes onto the sugar" as the tell. Glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase also adds a phosphate (inorganic phosphate, no ATP), so phrase the tell as a first-half kinase moving a phosphate from ATP, or it points at the payoff pair.

items.concept: Carriers enter the chain at different points: NADH at complex I (about 2.5 ATP), FADH2 at complex II, which skips complex I's pumping (about 1.5 ATP).
reasoning: Keep the two carriers on separate lines: FADH2 enters past complex I, so it earns less.

routes.15: NADH only, FADH2 left out (6 x 2.5)
routes.20: adds the 2 GTP made in the cycle (18 + 2), or FADH2 at the NADH rate (8 x 2.5)
routes.24: all eight carriers at the old whole-number 3 (8 x 3)

recompute.oldValues: 3 per NADH and 2 per FADH2 give 22, which is not a choice

choices.misconception: Gives every carrier the FADH2 rate: 8 x 1.5.
Counts the 6 NADH and leaves the 2 FADH2 out.
Adds the 2 GTP the cycle makes directly, which the stem excludes (from those carriers alone). Counting FADH2 at 2.5 lands here too.
Counts all eight carriers at the old whole-number value of 3.

writerNotes: The bank trap note for 20 calls 3 per NADH and 1 per FADH2 the older textbook values. The older values were 3 and 2 (giving 22). Do not carry that note into the explainer; use one of the routes in recompute.
Two clean steps with friendly numbers: meets the light-math rule as is.

items.expertAnswer: It slows, because the gradient builds and pumping against it gets harder
items.servedKey: It slows, because the gradient builds and pumping against it gets harder
items.concept: Respiratory control (chemiosmotic coupling): the chain and ATP synthase are linked through the proton gradient, so blocking the synthase backs up the chain.
reasoning: Trace the protons: the chain pumps them out of the matrix, and ATP synthase is their way back in.
Plug the synthase and protons pile up in the intermembrane space; the gradient steepens.
Pumping against a steeper gradient gets harder, so electron flow and oxygen use slow.

choices.text: It increases, because protons are no longer being used up
choices.misconception: Speeding up is what an uncoupler does by draining the gradient. A plug keeps the gradient full, which slows the pumps.

choices.text: It slows, because the gradient builds and pumping against it gets harder
choices.why: The gradient couples the two halves.

choices.text: It is unchanged, because the chain and ATP synthase work independently of each other
choices.misconception: Reads "complexes untouched" and stops there, missing the coupling through the gradient.

choices.text: It slows, because oxygen can no longer accept electrons
choices.misconception: It does slow, but that reason belongs to a complex IV poison such as cyanide, not to oligomycin.

choices.text: It increases briefly and then stops as the matrix becomes acidic
choices.misconception: Protons are pumped out of the matrix, so the matrix grows less acidic, not more.

items.expertAnswer: Fermentation uses no electron transport chain and builds no proton gradient
items.servedKey: Fermentation uses no electron transport chain and builds no proton gradient
items.concept: Anaerobic respiration keeps the chain and gradient with a non-oxygen final acceptor; fermentation has no chain or gradient and hands NADH's electrons to an organic molecule.
reasoning: Ask where NADH's electrons go.
Anaerobic respiration: into a membrane chain ending at sulfate or nitrate, building a gradient that drives ATP synthase.
Fermentation: straight to an organic molecule (pyruvate or acetaldehyde), no chain and no gradient, only the 2 ATP from glycolysis.

choices.text: Fermentation uses a chain too, but with oxygen as the final acceptor
choices.misconception: A chain ending at oxygen is aerobic respiration.

choices.text: Fermentation uses no electron transport chain and builds no proton gradient
choices.why: The chain and gradient are what set anaerobic respiration apart.

choices.text: It produces less ATP per glucose than fermentation does
choices.misconception: A chain plus a gradient out-earns fermentation, which keeps only glycolysis's 2 ATP.

choices.text: Fermentation passes electrons to nitrate, while anaerobic respiration passes them to pyruvate
choices.misconception: Swaps the two acceptors; the stem itself gives nitrate and sulfate to the chain-using bacteria.

choices.text: It is the same process under a different name
choices.misconception: Treats the two oxygen-free pathways as one because both run without oxygen.

items.expertAnswer: Fewer aquaporins in the collecting duct, so more dilute urine is produced
items.servedKey: Fewer aquaporins in the collecting duct, so more dilute urine is produced
items.concept: ADH inserts aquaporin water channels in the collecting duct; less ADH means less water reabsorbed and more, dilute urine.
reasoning: Name the hormone's job: ADH puts aquaporin water channels into the collecting duct.
Inhibit ADH release and fewer channels are inserted, so water stays in the tubule.
Result: more urine, and more dilute.

choices.text: Less glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule
choices.misconception: Glucose spills when blood glucose overwhelms the proximal transporters, as in diabetes mellitus. ADH does not handle glucose.

choices.text: A higher filtration rate at the glomerulus with no change in urine concentration
choices.misconception: Filtration is a nearby step ADH does not set, and urine concentration is exactly what changes.

choices.text: More aquaporins in the collecting duct, so less urine is produced
choices.misconception: That is ADH present. Inhibiting its release runs the other way.

choices.text: Fewer aquaporins in the collecting duct, so more dilute urine is produced
choices.why: No ADH, fewer water channels, water stays in the urine.

choices.text: More Na+ reabsorption in the distal tubule, so blood pressure rises
choices.misconception: That is aldosterone's effect, the neighboring hormone.

items.expertAnswer: The neuron can no longer fire action potentials
items.servedKey: The neuron can no longer fire action potentials
items.concept: The action potential upstroke is carried by voltage-gated Na+ channels; the resting potential is set by K+ leak channels and the Na+/K+ pump.
reasoning: Name the channel's job: voltage-gated Na+ channels carry the rising phase of the action potential.
Block them and no Na+ rushes in, so no spike can start.
The resting potential stays near normal, because the K+ leak and the pump are untouched.

choices.text: Neurotransmitter release increases at the terminal
choices.misconception: No action potential reaches the terminal, so release falls.

choices.text: The resting potential immediately rises to 0 mV
choices.misconception: The resting potential belongs to the K+ leak channels and the pump, which the toxin leaves alone.

choices.text: The neuron fires action potentials continuously
choices.misconception: Continuous firing is what a toxin that holds Na+ channels open does; this one blocks them.

choices.text: Repolarization fails, so the membrane stays positive
choices.misconception: Repolarization is the K+ channels' job, and here the spike never starts.

choices.text: The neuron can no longer fire action potentials
choices.why: No Na+ entry means no upstroke.

items.expertAnswer: It fires action potentials more frequently
items.servedKey: It fires action potentials more frequently
items.concept: Action potentials are all or none, so one neuron codes stimulus strength by firing frequency (and more neurons are recruited).
reasoning: Know the rule: every action potential is all or none, the same height and shape.
So a single neuron signals a stronger stimulus by firing more often.

choices.text: The resting potential becomes more negative
choices.misconception: A stronger stimulus depolarizes; a more negative rest would make firing harder.

choices.text: It fires action potentials more frequently
choices.why: Strength is coded as firing frequency.

choices.misconception: Bigger input, bigger output holds for graded potentials; the action potential is the all-or-none exception.

choices.text: The action potential travels faster down the same axon
choices.misconception: Speed is set by axon diameter and myelin: a different axon, not a stronger stimulus.
A receptor (graded) potential lasts as long as the stimulus; the action potential's duration is fixed by channel kinetics.
